nodes.content: Develop a subsurface two-phase flow surrogate that preserves local mass conservation while generalizing across unseen permeability connectivity.
requirements: Maximum cellwise mass-balance error stays below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep.
On unseen channel connectivity, breakthrough-time error remains below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver.

nodes.content: Train a transmissibility-aware graph network to predict phase fluxes and saturation increments, then project fluxes onto finite-volume continuity constraints.
How can predicted phase fluxes satisfy cellwise continuity without distorting breakthrough timing on unseen channel connectivity?
Transmissibility-weighted flux projection will keep peak cellwise residual below 0.1% of step injection and unseen-connectivity breakthrough error below 5%.
Benchmark flux projection on 200 held-out channel topologies against converged finite volumes, measuring peak cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error.
Across 200 held-out channel topologies, peak cellwise residual was 0.06% of timestep injection; maximum breakthrough-time error was 4.7%.
Retain transmissibility-weighted projection because both held-out worst-case metrics meet acceptance limits, despite breakthrough error nearing 5%.
Using retained projection, train with rewired channels; compare peak cellwise residual and breakthrough error against finite volumes on independent topologies.
Train projected graph surrogate on 10,000 rewired-channel cases; score mass residual and breakthrough error on 100 independent finite-volume simulations.
ChannelFlow-v1 checkpoint and 100-case benchmark report with peak cellwise mass residuals and finite-volume breakthrough-time comparisons.
Rerun ChannelFlow-v1 on the 100-case benchmark and independently recompute peak cellwise mass residual and maximum breakthrough-time error.
ChannelFlow-v1 on 100 independent topologies: peak cellwise residual 0.05% of timestep injection; maximum breakthrough-time error 4.1% versus finite volumes.
Uniform-weight flux projection will keep peak cellwise residual below 0.1% but raise maximum breakthrough-time error above 5% on unseen connectivity.
Replace transmissibility weights with uniform weights in ChannelFlow-v1; rerun the 100-case benchmark and compare both worst-case metrics.
Uniform projection: 0.05% peak cellwise residual of injected mass per timestep; maximum breakthrough-time error 4.6%, versus weighted 4.1%.
Embed a graph-conditioned relative-permeability closure in an implicit two-phase finite-volume solver with shared conservative face fluxes.
Can a graph-conditioned relative-permeability closure capture unseen-channel breakthrough while implicit finite-volume updates preserve cellwise phase mass?
Train graph-conditioned closure on rewired channels; embed in implicit finite volumes and benchmark phase-mass residuals and breakthrough on unseen topologies.
Train graph-conditioned closure on 10,000 rewired cases; assess implicit-solver mass residual and breakthrough on ChannelFlow-v1's 100-case benchmark.
ClosureFV-v1 checkpoint, implicit finite-volume integration code, and 100-topology report of cellwise phase-mass residuals and breakthrough-time errors.
Rerun ClosureFV-v1 and ChannelFlow-v1 on 100 shared topologies; compare maximum cellwise mass residuals and breakthrough-time errors against finite volumes.
ClosureFV-v1: peak cellwise phase-mass residual 0.02% of timestep injection; maximum breakthrough error 3.6%, versus ChannelFlow-v1’s 0.05% and 4.1%.
Select ClosureFV-v1 over ChannelFlow-v1: both meet acceptance limits, but ClosureFV-v1 has lower worst-case mass residual and breakthrough error.
A local-only ClosureFV-v1 closure retains <0.1% cellwise mass residual but exceeds 5% breakthrough-time error on unseen branching channels.
Using ClosureFV-v1 integration code, retrain a local-only closure and benchmark worst-case mass residual and breakthrough error on unseen branching channels.
On 40 unseen branching channels, local-only closure reached 0.03% peak cellwise mass residual but 8.2% maximum breakthrough error.
Learn permeability-graph multiscale pressure bases, then reconstruct face fluxes conservatively and advance saturations with finite-volume updates.
Graph-adaptive pressure bases will yield <0.1% peak cellwise mass residual and <5% maximum breakthrough error on unseen channels.
How many graph-adaptive pressure modes are needed to resolve bottleneck-controlled breakthrough on unseen channel topologies?
Sweep 8–64 graph-adaptive pressure modes on 40 unseen branching channels; compare worst-case mass residual and breakthrough error against finite volumes.
On 40 unseen branching channels, 8–64 modes yielded ≤0.04% peak mass residual but ≥6.3% maximum breakthrough error.
Thirty-two graph-adaptive modes plus eight bottleneck-localized modes will yield <5% maximum breakthrough error and <0.1% peak cellwise residual.
Add eight bottleneck-localized modes to the 32-mode surrogate; rerun 40 branching-channel cases and compute worst-case breakthrough and mass residuals.
On 40 branching channels, 32+8 modes achieved 0.04% peak cellwise residual, but maximum breakthrough-time error was 5.4%.
After 32+8's 5.4% error, 32 adaptive plus 16 bottleneck modes should yield <5% maximum breakthrough error and <0.1% cellwise residual.
Test 32 adaptive plus 16 bottleneck modes on 40 branching channels; measure maximum breakthrough error and peak cellwise residual.
On 40 branching channels, 32+16 modes achieved 0.04% peak cellwise residual and 4.8% maximum breakthrough-time error.
Use ClosureFV-v1’s 100-topology benchmark to test 32+16 modes’ maximum breakthrough-time error and peak cellwise mass residual against finite volumes.
On ClosureFV-v1’s 100-topology benchmark, 32+16 modes gave 0.04% peak cellwise residual and 4.9% maximum breakthrough-time error.
Retain 32+16 modes over 32+8: both benchmarks meet acceptance limits, while 32+8 misses the breakthrough limit.
Train a topology-conditioned streamline travel-time network to predict normalized face-transfer fractions, then update saturation using antisymmetric finite-volume fluxes.
Can topology-conditioned streamline travel times capture bypass routes on unseen channels while antisymmetric face transfers preserve cellwise mass?
Streamline travel-time conditioning will keep peak cellwise mass residual below 0.1% and maximum unseen-channel breakthrough error below 5%.
Train the travel-time network on 10,000 rewired channels; evaluate mass residuals and breakthrough errors on 100 unseen finite-volume cases.
On 100 unseen channels, peak cellwise residual was 0.07% of timestep injection; maximum breakthrough-time error was 4.4%.
Test the streamline surrogate on 40 unseen branching channels against converged finite volumes, recording worst-case mass residual and breakthrough error.
On 40 branching channels, peak cellwise residual was 0.08% of timestep injection, but maximum breakthrough-time error reached 7.1%.
Adding permeability-weighted alternate-path travel times will lower branching-channel maximum breakthrough error below 5% while preserving <0.1% peak cellwise residual.
Ablate alternate-path travel times on the 40 branching channels; compare both variants’ maximum breakthrough error and peak cellwise residual.
At half timestep on 40 branching channels, baseline reached 4.7% maximum breakthrough error; alternate-path reached 5.6%; both residuals stayed ≤0.08%.
Using ClosureFV-v1’s benchmark, compare baseline and alternate-path models at half timestep across 100 topologies for peak residual and breakthrough error.
At half timestep on 100 topologies, baseline and alternate-path breakthrough errors were 4.0% and 5.3%; peak residuals stayed ≤0.08%.
Benchmark alternate-path travel times at the original timestep on ClosureFV-v1’s 100 topologies, measuring peak mass residual and maximum breakthrough error.
On ClosureFV-v1’s 100 cases at original timestep, branching maximum breakthrough error fell 6.2%→4.7%; peak cellwise residual was 0.07%.
Use baseline at half timestep and alternate-path at original timestep; each meets limits where the other exceeds breakthrough tolerance.
Predict pressure using a permeability-conditioned operator, correct discrete residuals, and advance both phases through shared finite-volume fluxes.
Can discrete pressure-residual correction prevent unseen channel junctions from shifting breakthrough while maintaining conservative phase updates?
Two pressure-residual correction sweeps will achieve <0.1% peak cellwise mass residual and <5% maximum breakthrough error on unseen junctions.
Run two pressure-residual correction sweeps on 40 unseen junction topologies; measure peak cellwise mass residual and maximum breakthrough-time error.
On 40 unseen junctions, two correction sweeps yielded 0.06% peak cellwise residual and 4.8% maximum breakthrough-time error.
Benchmark two-sweep pressure correction on 100 independent unseen topologies against converged finite volumes, including junction-rich cases.
On 100 independent topologies, two correction sweeps kept peak cellwise residual at 0.07%, but maximum breakthrough error reached 5.5%.
Four pressure-residual correction sweeps will reduce maximum breakthrough error below 5% across 100 unseen topologies while retaining <0.1% peak residual.
Compare two versus four correction sweeps on the 100 unseen topologies, recording maximum breakthrough-time error and peak cellwise mass residual.
On 100 topologies, two/four sweeps yielded 5.5%/5.2% maximum breakthrough errors; two sweeps retained 4.8% on 40 junctions; residuals ≤0.07%.
Run four correction sweeps on ClosureFV-v1’s 100-topology benchmark; measure maximum breakthrough error and peak cellwise mass residual.
On ClosureFV-v1’s 100 topologies, four sweeps yielded 0.06% peak cellwise residual and 4.6% maximum breakthrough-time error.
Retain four sweeps for ClosureFV-v1’s benchmark (4.6% breakthrough error), but flag failure on independent topologies (5.2%).
Retain four sweeps; train on junction-rewired graphs, then retest 100 independent topologies for mass residual and breakthrough error.
Use ClosureFV-v1’s integration code for references; retrain the four-sweep operator on junction rewires; test 100 independent topologies.
JunctionPressure-v2 checkpoint and 100-topology benchmark report with four-sweep mass-residual and finite-volume breakthrough comparisons.
Reproduce JunctionPressure-v2’s 100-case report from its checkpoint; independently check peak cellwise mass residual and maximum breakthrough error.
JunctionPressure-v2 on 100 independent topologies: peak cellwise residual 0.06% of timestep injection; maximum breakthrough error 4.7%.
Adopt retrained four-sweep JunctionPressure-v2: independent-topology breakthrough error falls from 5.2% to 4.7%, with 0.06% peak mass residual.
